title: Song of the Grass-Roof Hermitage, Lines 19-22
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: The talk highlights the importance of sitting meditation (zazen) as a fundamental aspect of Zen practice, where one cultivates mindfulness and attention to let go of thoughts and distractions, allowing for a state of "not knowing" to arise. This involves embodying complete understanding and realization, rather than just learning meditation techniques. By bringing awareness and beginner's mind to the present moment, we can align with the bodhisattva path and manifest wholesome karma in daily life, without needing external teachings or methods.

All right.
Let's bow in, and then I'll ring a bell and we'll sit for two minutes.
If you could turn on the closed captions.
And Bob?
Yes.
Shall we do the beginning of a dharma talk first and then chant?
Okay, good.
All right.
*Unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in 100,000 million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tathagata's words.*
I am going to read the poem tonight.
Bob and I talked about having everybody read the poem, and it doesn't work to have us all read it.
So if you would allow me, I will read it.
Okay with that, Bob?
Okay.
Please read along with me, and let's unmute everyone.
I'll do that.
*I've built a grass hut where there's nothing of value.
After eating, I relax and enjoy a nap.
When it was completed, fresh weeds appeared.
Now it's been lived in, covered by weeds.
The person in the hut lives here calmly, not stuck to inside, outside or in between.
Places worldly people live, he doesn't live.
Realms worldly people love, he doesn't love.
Though the hut is small, it includes the entire world.*
*In 10 feet square, an old man illumines forms and their nature.
A great vehicle Bodhisattva trusts without doubt.
The middling or lowly can't help wondering, will this hut perish or not?
Perishable or not, the original master is present.
Not dwelling, south or north, east or west, firmly based on steadfastness, it can't be surpassed.
A shining window below the green pines.
Jade palaces or vermilion towers can't compare with it.
Just sitting with head covered, all things are at rest.
Thus, this mountain monk doesn't understand at all.*
*Living here, he no longer works to get free.
Who would proudly arrange seats, trying to entice guests?
Turn around the light to shine within, then just return.
The vast, inconceivable source can't be faced or turned away from.
Meet the ancestral teachers, be familiar with their instruction.
Bind grasses to build a hut and don't give up.
Let go of hundreds of years and relax completely.
Open your hands and walk, innocent.*
*Thousands of words, myriad interpretations are only to free you from abstractions, from obstructions.
If you want to know the undying person in the hut, don't separate from this skin bag, here and now.*
Good evening, friends and fellow Bodhisattvas.
Tonight we're going to have another opening story about Sherdu.

After Master Ching Wan's passing, after his teacher's passing, Sherdu traveled to the southern peak, Nanyue, in the Hang Mountain region of Hunan, and built a grass thatched hut for himself on a stone ledge that was exposed on the side of a hill.
Because of his hermitage on the rock, he soon became known as Sherdu Heishang, monk rockytop.
Having settled close to his spiritual uncle, Nanyue Huairang, the two are almost certain to have been in contact.
One account in the Ancestors' Hall collection records a conversation between Shi Xian and Master Nanyue.
Shi Xian is Sherdu's second name.
Shi Xian asked, "What do we do when teachers are no longer needed, but one's understanding hasn't been recognized?"
Nanyue said, "That's a bit arrogant.
How about asking something more humble?"
Shi Xian said, "Even being reborn endlessly, we can't reach liberation by following others."
Master Nanyue was silent.
Shi Xian departed.

Later, an attendant monk came and reported to Master Nanyue, "The monk who came to ask you questions recently, the one who was quite disrespectful, he's now practicing on a rock ledge to the east of here."
The master told the attendant, "Go over and tell him that a person of such strong intention would be welcome to practice here in our temple."
The attendant delivered the message, but Shi Xian declined the offer.
Nanyue said, "Nobody will ever get the better of this man."
Master Nanyue later helped to arrange the building of a small temple for Shi Xian near the site of his hut.
Shi Xian soon began to attract students and, known as Master Shirdu, eventually became one of the most influential teachers in the Zen tradition.
In the classes up ahead, we'll talk a little bit about the tradition that Shirdu and Matsu developed, the five, what are now called the five schools of Zen.
Now a few short encounter dialogues to frame up today's verse we're going to read.
Shirdu has this method of always posing a question that seems to strip away all thinking.
Once a monk named Shili asked, "What are monks supposed to do?"
Master Shirdu said, "What are you asking me for?"
Shili said, "If I don't ask you, how can I find the truth?"
And Shirdi said, "Are you sure you've lost it?"
The monk Dawu once asked, "Who has attained the essential principle of the teacher of [unclear: "Khaozi"] or Huineng?"
Master Shirdi said, "The one who understands the teachings of Buddhism."
Dawu asked, "Then have you attained it?"
The master said, "I haven't attained it."
And Dawu asked, "Why not?"
Master said, "Because I don't understand Buddhism."
Another time, Dawu asked, "What is the fundamental teaching of the Buddha way?"
Master Shirdi said, "Not attaining, not knowing.
You already have it."
Dawu asked, "Is there anything beyond this?"
And the master said, "White clouds pass freely through the vast sky."
With that, to frame up tonight's verse:
*Just sitting with head covered, all things are at rest.
Thus, this mountain monk doesn't understand at all.
Living here, he no longer works to get free.
Who would proudly arrange seats, trying to entice guests?*

As I've been reading this poem over and over, as I'm sure you have as well, I think this is maybe the pivotal passage, from my perspective, of what this core activity is that we're all engaged in: sitting in zazen, practicing realization moment by moment.
Tonight I'd like to walk through some commentary on each of these lines and then open the floor for discussion.
Then we'll go to breakout rooms and have adequate time to really investigate the question.
The first line: sitting with head covered, all things are at rest.
One of the things that Ben Connolly stresses is that the security of having a roof over our head allows us to meditate.
I want to take it from the other direction, about what the act of sitting with that security means and what some of the teachings might help us understand.
Sitting with our head covered, I hear that immediately taken to our morning robe chant, putting our rakusu or yokesa on top of our heads.
That's the moment where we enter full practice.
Shenwa Michael Newton up in Mountain Rain points out that these guys had shaved heads.
It was cold.
You need to put something over your head to stay warm.
So there's a practical aspect to it as well.
But I've got this perspective, in the human context, of what our practice emphasizes, and both how ordinary it is and maybe how special it is.
I came across an interesting quote, in an article a couple of times, on the impact of technology and our attention span.
This is from 1654, from Blaise Pascal, a French philosopher.
He said, "All of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone."

This was the header for an NPR story earlier this year about college students who were asked to sit for 10 or 20 minutes without any technical devices, just to sit still and live with their own thoughts.
They were even given an initial training that they could give themselves an electric shock, and they found that unpleasant.

But nonetheless, by the end of the study, they found that 70 percent of the men and 25 percent of the women chose to shock themselves during the 12 minutes that they sat, rather than just sitting there and entertaining themselves with their thoughts.
Over half of the participants confessed to cheating, that is, to using their electronic devices during those 12 minutes.
They weren't supposed to get on their phones or talk to other people, but over half said they had, and the researchers said, "And those were just the ones that were honest with us."

So in the context of our sitting for 35 minutes, this is quite profound, what is happening to our minds and to our culture in terms of our ability to sit still and pay attention and to get to the point of non-thinking.
In the Fukanzazen of Dogen that we chant, it says:
*Think of not thinking.
How do you think of not thinking?
Non-thinking.
This in itself is the essential art of zazen.
The zazen I speak of is not learning meditation.
It is simply the Dharma gate of repose, endless, the practice realization of totally culminated enlightenment.*
Each time we totally engage in just sitting, practice absolutely means completely, totally all-inclusive.
It's everything.
There's nothing left over or left out of our zazen.
Each moment zazen is Buddha actualization, and there's no progress because there's nothing outside that moment of total engagement to compare it to.
Zazen is our actualization, our realization of not being separate.
So the notion of all things being at rest is something that we can come to, but it is something we definitely have to have an intention towards.
Thus this mountain monk doesn't understand at all.
This gets back to Suzuki Roshi's beginner's mind, the sense of humility, of total openness, of really trust that was spoken of earlier in the poem: a great Bodhisattva trusts without doubt.
Dogen reminds us that "thus" doesn't mean like something, it means exactly.
So these two lines together are really saying that in zazen it is exactly not understanding.
Our teacher, Zoketsu Norman Fischer, gave a talk on case 20 in the Book of Serenity, Dizhang's not knowing is most intimate.
He points out that when you train in being present and letting things come and go, you are training in not knowing, not understanding.
Within not knowing we make determinations and we take actions, but every moment calls on us to respond, and we do freely and with full confidence, trusting.
Sometimes affirmation is called for, sometimes denial.
There are no rules, but whichever it is, we don't just settle down there and get stuck.
We don't identify and dig in.
We stand in not knowing, ready for the next moment to be different, trusting without doubt.
Chris Burkhart can't be here because of technical difficulties, but on Monday nights some of us sit with her and read Dogen.
In one of those moments she brought up a commentary of Okumura's on the Mountains and Rivers Sutra, which suggests a couple of ways to approach this notion of not understanding.
When Dogen uses it as a compound, he doesn't say not understanding, he says do not understanding.
It's parallel to do not non-thinking: to go beyond understanding.
That is to embody and actually practice understanding without stagnating within understanding, or from another direction, letting go of not understanding.
Thought is understanding; by letting go we do not understanding.
This sitting and letting go of thought, this opening the hand of thought, a phrase that will come up later in this poem, is the true Dharma eye.
That means we're not grasping things with our karma consciousness.
The thing that struck me in this passage when Chris turned us to it was that this release is the completely unique activity of zazen.
In zazen we are determined not to take action based on the thoughts coming and going.
Therefore, this is the kicker, we don't create new karma.
In zazen we don't create new karma.
In ordinary life, thought leads to actions.
When we open the hand of thought we let go and no actions arise.
Only in zazen can we stop making karma.
**Joden Bob Rose:** Our practice in daily life is about creating wholesome karma.
In this context, wholesome karma means to manifest in daily life what we experience in zazen: no separation between ourselves and other people and the myriad things.
So we try to make moment-by-moment choices that are in the direction of our bodhisattva path.
This last year I had the happy occasion to finally enter the world of Barry Lopez.
In reading a book of his essays called Horizon, I came across a passage about what understanding means from another cultural perspective altogether.
He's out hunting up in the Arctic with some indigenous people.
And he says he's learned a couple of lessons about how to be more present, how to be more fully present in an encounter with a wild animal or whatever the next occasion is in this life.
*I needed to understand that I was entering the event as it was unfolding.
It started before I arrived and would continue unfolding after I departed.
That's the first lesson.
The second is, let's say we didn't disturb the grizzly bear as he fed but only took in what he or she was doing and slid away.
The event itself could not be completely defined by referring solely to the physical geography around us in those moments.
My friends had situated themselves within a dynamic event.

The lesson in those experiences would not just for me to pay closer attention to what was going on around me, if I have hope to have a deeper understanding, but to remain in a state of suspended mental analysis while observing all that was happening, resisting the urge to define or summarize, to step away from the familiar compulsion to understand.*

In a sense, that's a good parallel to our zazen practice, just like those indigenous hunters, how they view the world around us unfolding as a dynamic event and not trying to hang on to the moment and try to understand it.
The next line is:
*Living here, he no longer works to get free.*
The actual character translated for "here" is the hut itself that we've spoken of before.
The term "to get free" is really "to untie," with the same root as "to tie," and the opening stanza is about tying together grasses to make a grass hut.
So in a way what this line is saying, I think, is he doesn't need to have any explanations.
He's not trying to get out.
He's not trying to leave the situation.
He's fully embracing his hut, fully embracing his body, his mind, his situation.
He's relaxed, but he's not lazy.
I think there are multiple ways to read "no longer works."
He's already free, so he doesn't have to work to get free.
He's no longer working at it.
He's given up working on freeing himself, or he's given into the non-karma-creating moment of just sitting with no sense of discomfort.
Or he realizes there's nothing to free himself from in light of all these things at rest when sitting, or he's just relaxing where he is, eating his rice and taking a nap.
Suzuki Roshi reminds us that we must make some effort.
This is not being lazy, but we must forget ourselves in the effort we make.
A monk once asked Shurdu, "How does one get emancipated?"
The master said, "Who has ever put you in bondage?"
The monk asked, "What is the pure land?"
And the master said, "Who has ever defiled you?"
And finally, the monk asked, "What is nirvana?"
And Shurdu said, "Who has ever subjected you to birth and death?"
And the final line of this stanza is:
*Who would proudly arrange seats trying to entice guests?*
It's one of the more mysterious lines in the poem.
Another way to translate it would be, "Who spreads out and arranges mats for somebody to buy something, as if it's in the marketplace?"
Or, "Who boastfully spreads out a map aiming for customers?"
The character that's translated in our translation as "proud" can also be "to boast," "to exaggerate," "to praise."
So there's this notion of someone who's being self-reflective, ego-driven, not self-contained.
Certainly not a vessel with no leakage, as our teachings say.
And this idea of hosts and guests really shows up first in the teachings, in the dialogue with the Buddha in the Surangamma Sutra.
The World-Honored One supposes a question from one of his disciples.
*Suppose a visitor stops at an inn for a night or for a meal.
Once his stay is ended or the meal is finished, he packs his bags and goes on his way.
He's not at leisure to remain, but if he were the innkeeper, he would not leave.
By considering this example of the visitor, the one who comes and goes, and the innkeeper, the one who remains, I understood what the visitor signifies.
He represents transience.
Also, a good host does not interfere with his guest.
The guest signifies the part of our mind with a million thoughts, and the host is the part which is before thought.*
So as this tradition evolves from Shurju to Dongshan to Dogen, Dongshan has a whole teaching on the five ranks that have to do with the relationship of the host and guest.
This is far more complicated than I can even touch on tonight, but this is part of a very deep consideration in our practice.
But the question is, who would put out these chairs and mattresses?
What conditions would change to make this the right way to present to the world?
What doubt would arise for this trusting monk to have to do that?

If the host, as we were talking earlier in the poem, the original master, is always present, and the guests are our thoughts, our desires, our sufferings, and if, in fact, you're sitting and all things are at rest, why would you need to entice guests?
They certainly will come on their own, but you don't have to do anything to allow that to happen.
So why bother [unclear: "airs"] trying to create a special place, especially after it seems we've rejected the whole idea of jade palaces and the million towers as being somehow attractive?
If our monk doesn't understand, if we don't understand, why would we even consider offering something like teachings, which Shurju is definitely averse to?
People had to come to him.
He wasn't out there saying, "I'm teaching this new method here on my rock."
He didn't want to teach people anything.
If they came, he would sit with them, but that wasn't his deal.
So what is the need to sell or propose or offer anything?
Our practice is to bring it to life on the cushion where we sit.
Just to summarize it, our master Dogen reminds us, and Suzuki Roshi, our practice is enlightenment, and where we practice, we enact beginner's mind.
As I've looked at these four verses, it seems that's been a core of what this whole poem is about.
With that, I think we'll open up the floor for some comments.
Then in a few minutes, Hanna will ring a bell and we'll go into breakout rooms to discuss the question, which is: how and where do we practice and find contentment?
And how do we bring that practice into our lives and communicate with others?
Or do we communicate with others at all about it?
Do we set out a mat and tell people what our practice is, or do we just practice?
So the floor is open for comments, and then Hanna will ring the bell and we'll go to breakout rooms and come back and have a few minutes after that.
**Participant:** Well, first line, Bob, what do you make of "head covered"?
Seems like the logical thing is this thing, and what Ben interprets it as is just sitting under cover.
But why is it "head covered"?
**Joden Bob Rose:** Well, I think that it may be the ambiguity of the translation.
The translation actually talks about a robe, putting on a robe.
Pull that out here.
There's a kind of shorthand that inevitably comes to bear in these.
Yeah, the characters are like: take a robe, shelter, head, innumerable duties.
Right.
Yeah, the 10,000 duties or the 10,000 affairs.
And they stop, and they stop and rest.
Stop.
Do not retire.
Put it on your robe and hang out under shelter and everything stops.
Yeah.
I wonder why "head covered."
Anyway, let's just argue with the translator though.
**Participant:** I wondered that too.
And when Bob said early on this evening he thought of putting our [unclear: "wreck-a-soos"] on our heads, that really did mean something to me.
Suddenly that opened that up a little bit.
I thought about it meaning just turning inward, not paying so much attention to the external world, but looking inside.
Like if you really cover your head so you can't see around you, something like that.
Inward glance.
Yeah, there we go.
I think you're right on the button.
You know, when I put a hood up, I have that feeling of a little bit more insular, peacefulness, shutting out outside things, maybe a little bit safer.
Hooded robe was used in just about all the traditions.
I think maybe for that reason.
And look at, I mean, they've been using blinders for horses for a thousand years just for that reason of shutting out transient things.
And we're already in a hut to begin with.
So it's a doubling down of that privacy or containment.
So on page 117, Connolly says, can you guys hear me?
Okay.
Okay.
He says, "Oh, by dampening the dominance of the mind, he exposes the body and the senses."
That line really spoke to me, that idea that you're quelling all of the thoughts and allowing it to move into a more somatic experience.
Which is my take on it.
You know, I had a reaction to the head covering thing too.
And I had to step back for a while.
I had a kind of traumatic experience at Tassajara because I would walk into the zendo with my hat on.
And it was a very, very bad thing.
I probably did that about three times and always got reprimanded for it.
We don't wear head covering, you know, we don't wear that in our tradition.
And so I have the same reaction Tim did: what is that doing there?
And then I thought of Christian monks who, you know, you think of them with their hoods on, how they wear those hoods over their head.
But it's not something we do.
So I thought it was a bit too, I don't know.
I don't have any more thoughts on that.
When you see paintings of Bodhidharma, he's got part of his attire is a hood over his head.
That's right.
It's cold in those caves if your head's shaved.
Many of the rules changed later on.
So I'm going to step in here and say let's go to breakout rooms.
Did you post the questions?
I am posting the question right now.
Thank you.
And I'm going to send you all into your breakout rooms.
And we'll come back at 20 minutes after the hour.
Right?
Yep.
We have 15 minutes to be in a breakout room.
Bob, you can either go into your breakout room or not.
Yeah, sure.
Yeah, I'd like to.
